title: Landscape quote checker
text: Enter your area, the depth you want, and up to three quotes. The checker shows the depth each quote would actually cover, whether it’s more (or less) than you need, and the price per unit, so quotes in yards, tons and bags can be compared fairly.

title: Landscape quote checker
text:
Yards and tons converter
Soil and mulch are usually sold by the cubic yard; stone, gravel and sand by the ton. This converts between them, and shows what an amount will cover.

title: Landscape quote checker
section: Why quotes are hard to compare
text:
Why quotes are hard to compare

Yards vs tons. A cubic yard of mulch weighs a few hundred pounds; a cubic yard of gravel weighs well over a ton. A price per ton and a price per yard can’t be compared unless you know what the material weighs. The checker converts using typical weights; ask the supplier for theirs.
Delivery. A delivery fee spread over a small load makes the price per unit look high. Compare quotes for the same quantity.
Extra for settling. Loose material settles after spreading, so a fair quote includes a little more than the measured volume, usually 5–25% depending on the material. A quote for double what you need is not “a little extra”.
Bags. Bag sizes vary (1, 1.5, 2 or 3 cubic feet). Check the bag size before comparing bag prices.

Use the materials calculator to work out exactly how much you need for an odd-shaped area.

title: Sprinkler catch-cup test
text:
Most people guess their sprinkler run times. A catch-cup test measures what each zone actually puts down, in about 20 minutes, with a few cups and a ruler.
How to do it: set out 8–12 identical straight-sided containers (tuna cans or plastic cups) in a grid across one zone, away from the heads themselves. Run the zone for 10–20 minutes. Measure the water depth in each container with a ruler and enter them below.

title: Sprinkler catch-cup test
text:
What the numbers mean

Application rate is how fast the zone puts water down. Spray heads are usually fast (1–2 in/hr); rotors and rotary nozzles are slow (0.3–0.7 in/hr). Zones with different head types need different run times.
Evenness (DU) compares the driest quarter of the cups with the average. At 70% or above, coverage is good. Below about 55%, some spots get less than half as much as others, and adding minutes just floods the wet spots to rescue the dry ones.
Scheduling multiplier. Because coverage is never perfect, the run time is stretched a little so the drier areas still get enough. Better coverage means a smaller multiplier and less water.

Repeat the test for each zone: zones rarely match. Once you know a zone’s rate, the cycle-and-soak scheduler checks whether your soil can absorb it that fast.

title: Cycle-and-soak sprinkler scheduler
text: If water runs down the sidewalk while the sprinklers are on, your heads are putting water down faster than the soil can take it in. The fix costs nothing: run the same total time in shorter cycles, with a soak in between. This works out how short, and how many.

title: Cycle-and-soak sprinkler scheduler
text:
Why this works
Water soaks into soil at a limited rate. Sandy soil can take in an inch or more an hour; clay may take in a tenth of an inch. Spray heads often put down over an inch an hour, so on clay most of a long cycle runs off. On slopes it runs off even sooner.
Short cycles stop each round before water starts to run off; the soak lets it move down into the soil before the next round. The total water is the same; you just stop losing it to the gutter.
The intake rates used here are typical design values for each soil and slope. Compacted soil or a hard layer near the surface (very common on new-build lots) cuts them sharply. If you still see runoff, shorten the cycles further.

title: Soil test translator
text: Copy the numbers from your soil test report. You don’t need all of them: leave blanks for anything your report doesn’t have. The translator explains each result and, just as usefully, tells you what you don’t need to buy.

title: Soil test translator
text:
Getting a soil test
Most state university extension services run soil tests for home gardeners at low cost, as do many private labs. Ask for a routine or garden test: it usually covers pH, organic matter, salts, phosphorus, potassium and often nitrate.

Sample right. Take 10–15 small cores from across the area, 0–6 in deep for gardens and 0–4 in for lawns, mix them in a clean bucket, and send about two cups.
Sample areas separately. A vegetable bed, a lawn and a shrub border are different soils with different needs.
Every 3–4 years is enough for most gardens, unless you’re fixing a problem.

A soil test is the cheapest way to avoid buying fertilizer, compost or lime you don’t need.

title: Landscape materials calculator
text: Measure your area, pick a material, and see how much to order: in cubic yards, tons, bags or pallets. Odd shapes are fine: add them up piece by piece and subtract patios or paths. Every number shows how it was calculated, so you can check it against a supplier’s quote.

title: Landscape materials calculator
text:
How to measure

Rectangles and squares: length × width. An L-shaped bed is two rectangles; add them as two pieces.
Circles: measure straight across the middle (the diameter). For a ring around a tree, add the full circle and subtract the inner circle.
Triangles: measure all three sides. You don’t need the height.
Curvy beds: run a tape measure along the longest straight line through the bed. Every few feet, measure straight across at a right angle. Enter those widths in order, including both ends (0 if the bed comes to a point). The more widths you measure, the more accurate the area.

title: Landscape materials calculator
section: Why order more than you measured
text:
Why order more than you measured
Loose soil, compost and mulch settle once they are spread and watered, and road base or sand shrinks when it is compacted. The calculator adds a typical allowance for each material; you can change it under Assumptions. It then rounds up to the next half unit, because suppliers rarely sell less.

title: Landscape materials calculator
text:
Cubic yards vs tons
Soil, compost and mulch are usually sold by the cubic yard (volume). Stone, gravel and sand are usually sold by the ton (weight). The same cubic yard can weigh anywhere from about 600 lb (mulch) to over 2,500 lb (gravel), so a price per ton and a price per yard cannot be compared without knowing the weight. Ask your supplier what their material weighs per yard, and put that number in Assumptions.

title: Landscape materials calculator
text:
Before you buy topsoil
“Topsoil” has no legal definition, and quality varies a lot. Before you buy, ask:

Is it screened? Screened soil has had rocks, roots and clods removed.
What is in it? Native soil, a blend with compost or sand, or fill dirt?
Has it been tested? Ask for pH, organic matter, salts and texture. A reputable supplier can tell you.
Can I see it first? Look for weeds, construction debris, plastic or a sour smell. When the load arrives, check that it matches what you saw.

Don’t pay for more than you need: a quote for several times the volume this calculator gives is worth questioning.

title: Lawn vs low-water landscape: water use calculator
text: How much water does a lawn actually use compared with the alternatives? This estimates a season’s irrigation for the same area planted different ways, from your climate and water price.

title: Lawn vs low-water landscape: water use calculator
text:
How this is worked out
Plants lose water through their leaves at a rate set mainly by weather: sun, heat, wind and dry air. Weather networks express that as reference evapotranspiration (ETo): what a well-watered grass would use. Each planting uses a share of it: bluegrass close to 80%, buffalograss under half, established low-water shrubs a third or less. Subtract the rain the plants can use, allow for watering that’s never perfectly efficient, and you have the irrigation.
The factors used here are typical values for planning. They’re useful for comparing options, not for setting a controller: for that, use the catch-cup test.

title: Rain barrel and rainwater harvesting calculator
text: Roofs collect a surprising amount of water: an inch of rain on 1,000 ft² of roof is about 600 gallons. This works out what your roof collects and how that compares with a rain barrel.

title: Rain barrel and rainwater harvesting calculator
text:
Making the most of it

Barrels fill fast and empty slowly. Use the water between storms so there’s room for the next one.
A soaker hose or drip line works on barrel pressure if the barrel is raised on blocks; sprinklers don’t.
For larger volumes, directing downspouts into planted areas or a rain garden stores water in the soil itself, often more of it than barrels hold, and is allowed almost everywhere.

title: DIY soil tests: texture, drainage and the ribbon test
text: Three simple tests tell you most of what matters about your soil: what it’s made of (texture) and how fast water moves through it (drainage). Texture decides how often to water, how fast water soaks in, and how the soil behaves when you dig.

title: DIY soil tests: texture, drainage and the ribbon test
text:
Jar test (texture)

Fill a straight-sided jar about one-third with soil from root depth (pick out stones, roots and debris).
Add water until the jar is about two-thirds full, plus a teaspoon of dishwasher detergent or salt-free water softener to separate the particles.
Shake hard for 3–5 minutes, then set it down and start a timer.
After 1 minute, mark the height of the settled layer: that’s the sand.
After 2 hours, mark the height again: sand plus silt.
After 2 days (when the water clears), mark the final height: everything, including clay.

title: DIY soil tests: texture, drainage and the ribbon test
text:
Ribbon test (texture by feel)
Take a walnut-sized lump of soil, wet it until it’s like putty, and work it in your hand. Then press it between your thumb and finger, pushing it up into a ribbon until it breaks under its own weight.

title: DIY soil tests: texture, drainage and the ribbon test
text:
Drainage (percolation) test

Dig a hole about 12 in (30 cm) deep and 6–12 in wide.
Fill it with water and let it drain completely. This wets the surrounding soil; skip it and the result will be too fast.
Fill it again. Measure the water depth, wait a set time (an hour is easy), and measure again.



If the hole still holds water the next day, test again somewhere else and dig deeper to look for a dense or cemented layer. Drainage problems are usually about a layer below, not the soil you plant in.

title: Rain garden and dry well calculator
text: A rain garden is a shallow planted dip that catches runoff from a roof or driveway and lets it soak in. A dry well does the same job underground, in a pit filled with gravel. Both depend on how fast your soil drains, so do a drainage test first.

title: Rain garden and dry well calculator
text:
Building a rain garden

Location: a low spot at least 10 ft from the house, where water already heads, but not where it stands for days.
Shape: longer than it is wide, across the slope, with a level bottom so water spreads evenly.
Inlet and overflow: line the inlet with stone so it doesn’t erode, and give the overflow a safe path for storms bigger than the design.
Plants: wet-tolerant species in the bottom, drought-tolerant ones on the rim. Native plants with deep roots keep the soil open.
Soil: if your soil drains poorly, mix compost into the bottom, but don’t create a “bathtub” of loose soil in dense clay. An underdrain is the fix for very slow soils.

title: Tree protection zone calculator
text:
Most of a tree’s roots are in the top 12–18 inches of soil and spread well beyond the branches. Driving, stockpiling, trenching or changing the grade over them can kill a mature tree, often a few years later. Before any work, fence off a protection zone.
Measure the trunk at 4½ ft (1.4 m) above the ground. Wrap a tape around it for the circumference, or measure the diameter directly.

title: Tree protection zone calculator
text:
Why trees die after construction
Roots need air as much as water. Compaction from vehicles crushes the pore spaces; fill soil buries roots too deep; trenching cuts them. The tree may look fine for a season or two, using stored energy, then decline from the top down. By the time you see dieback, the damage was done years before.
The zone here scales with the trunk, the tree’s age and how well the species copes, following a widely used arborist approach. The simpler rule of thumb, one foot of radius per inch of trunk diameter, is shown in the working for comparison.

title: Soil pH calculator: lime and sulfur
text: Changing soil pH takes more material on clay than on sand, and it happens slowly. This estimates how much ground limestone (to raise pH) or elemental sulfur (to lower it) you need, and tells you when lowering pH isn’t realistic.

title: Soil pH calculator: lime and sulfur
text:
Why pH changes slowly
Soil is buffered: clay and organic matter hold large reserves of acidity (or alkalinity) that resist change. That’s why clay needs two or three times as much lime as sand, and why the same amount works slowly.
Lowering pH in alkaline soils is a special case. Many soils in dry regions contain free lime (calcium carbonate), which fizzes in vinegar. Any acid you add, including sulfur as it breaks down, is used up dissolving that lime before the pH moves. Even 1% lime takes well over 100 lb of sulfur per 1,000 ft² just to neutralise. That’s why gardeners in those regions do better choosing plants suited to their soil.
The rates here are typical extension values for the top 6 inches. A lab “lime requirement” or “buffer pH” result is more accurate for your soil when you have one.

title: Drip irrigation calculator
text: Drip puts water at the roots, but run times are usually guesses. Enter what each plant needs and what your emitters deliver; this works out the run time and checks that the zone can supply it.

title: Drip irrigation calculator
text:
Tips

Water deeply, less often. Infrequent, longer runs wet a deeper root zone than daily short ones, and deep roots handle heat better.
Emitters belong at the edge of the roots, not against the trunk or stem. For trees and shrubs that means moving them outward as the plant grows.
New plantings need more frequent water for their first season. Established native and low-water plants often need little or none outside drought.
Check the filter and flush the lines each spring. Clogged emitters are the most common reason a drip zone stops working.

title: Check a result
text: Before you submit, or when you review, check that the numbers can all be true. Each check takes the figures a paper or report gives (or your own) and tests them against what the method allows. Nothing you enter leaves your browser.

title: Check a result
text:
Finding the right pixel size
Grid resolution is often chosen by habit (30 m because that’s Landsat). Hengl (2006) set out rules that tie it to what the data can actually support. For each aspect of a dataset they give a coarsest legible resolution (the largest pixel that still represents it), a finest legible resolution (below which pixels “are probably just waste of memory”) and a recommended compromise. Fill in whatever you know; the overall range is where the rules agree.



Reference
Hengl, T. (2006). Finding the right pixel size. Computers & Geosciences 32, 1283–1298. doi:10.1016/j.cageo.2005.11.008

title: Check a result
text:
Back-transformation
A mean calculated on log values, then exponentiated, is the median (geometric mean), not the mean. For skewed soil properties the difference is often 10–30%. Enter what the paper gives on the log scale.



References
Aitchison, J., Brown, J.A.C. (1957). The Lognormal Distribution. Cambridge University Press.
Journel, A.G. (1980). The lognormal approach to predicting local distributions of selective mining unit grades. Mathematical Geology 12, 285–303. doi:10.1007/BF01029417
Webster, R., Oliver, M.A. (2007). Geostatistics for Environmental Scientists, 2nd ed. Wiley.

title: Check a result
text:
Carbon stock arithmetic
Rebuild a reported stock from its inputs. If it doesn’t match, the check tries the common slips (% vs g/kg, stones ignored or on the wrong basis, organic matter instead of carbon, kg/m² vs Mg/ha) and tells you which one reproduces the reported number.



References
Poeplau, C., Vos, C., Don, A. (2017). Soil organic carbon stocks are systematically overestimated by misuse of the parameters bulk density and rock fragment content. SOIL 3, 61–66. doi:10.5194/soil-3-61-2017
Pribyl, D.W. (2010). A critical review of the conventional SOC to SOM conversion factor. Geoderma 156, 75–83. doi:10.1016/j.geoderma.2010.02.003

title: Check a result
text:
Area from a confusion matrix
Counting pixels in a map gives biased class areas, because every map has errors. With a stratified accuracy sample, the confusion matrix gives unbiased areas with confidence intervals (Olofsson et al. 2014). Rows are map classes, columns are reference classes, and the last column is each map class’s mapped area.



Reference
Olofsson, P., Foody, G.M., Herold, M., Stehman, S.V., Woodcock, C.E., Wulder, M.A. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment 148, 42–57. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015

title: Check a result
text:
Effective sample size
Samples close together carry overlapping information. For estimating an average, a cluster of ten nearby samples can be worth little more than one. This uses the variogram to work out how many independent samples your layout is really worth.

Webster, R., Oliver, M.A. (2007). Geostatistics for Environmental Scientists, 2nd ed. Wiley.

Spatial cross-validation and leakage
Random cross-validation on spatial data usually tests points close to the training data, so it reports accuracy the map won’t achieve between samples. Tick anything that applies to the study you’re checking.

Results from different methods aren’t directly comparable. These are the common conversion factors, with the assumption behind each stated, so you can see what you’re accepting when you convert.

Oxide and unit conversions are exact, from molar masses.

title: Check a result
text:
Coordinates and distances
A degree of longitude shrinks with latitude, so distances calculated directly on longitude and latitude are distorted, and “metres” computed from degrees are wrong. Convert a distance, or paste coordinates to check them.



Method
No paper needed: standard spherical geometry (haversine formula, mean Earth radius 6,371 km).

title: Fertilizer label calculator
text: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag (N-P-K) are percentages by weight. A 20 lb bag of 24-0-6 contains 4.8 lb of nitrogen; the rest is the other nutrients and filler. This turns the label into how much product to spread, and shows what you’re really paying per pound of nutrient.

title: Fertilizer label calculator
text:
Reading a fertilizer label

N (nitrogen) drives green leafy growth. It’s the nutrient lawns need most, and it doesn’t stay in soil long, which is why it’s applied regularly.
P (phosphate, P₂O₅) supports roots and establishment. The label shows phosphate, not pure phosphorus: elemental P is about 44% of the P₂O₅ number.
K (potash, K₂O) helps with stress tolerance. Elemental K is about 83% of the K₂O number.
Slow-release or organic products feed over weeks rather than days. The arithmetic is the same; they’re just gentler.

More is not better. Extra nitrogen means more mowing, weaker roots and nitrate washing into waterways. A soil test tells you whether you need phosphate or potash at all.

title: Foundation grading check
text:
Water pooling against a foundation is one of the most expensive problems a house can have. The common building-code guideline is that ground should fall at least 6 inches over the first 10 feet from the house (about 5%). You can check it in an afternoon.
How to measure: drive a stake against the foundation and another 10 ft (3 m) out. Tie a string between them and level it with a line level. At each stake, measure from the string down to the ground. The drop is the outer measurement minus the inner one. Repeat every 10–15 ft along each wall.

title: Foundation grading check
section: Other signs of a grading problem
text:
Other signs of a grading problem

Water standing next to the foundation after rain or irrigation.
Mulch or soil piled up against the siding, often built up over years.
Downspouts that empty right at the wall.
Patios, walks or window wells that have settled so they tip toward the house.
Damp patches, efflorescence (white crust) or musty smells in a basement or crawlspace.

Most of these are cheap to fix compared with foundation repairs.

title: New-build yard soil check
text:
On many new-build lots, the topsoil is scraped off during construction, the subsoil is compacted by heavy machinery, and a thin layer of soil is spread back on top before the sod goes down. Lawns and plants then struggle for years. A few simple checks show whether that’s what happened.
You’ll need: a shovel, a long screwdriver, and moist (not soggy) soil, a day or two after rain or watering.

title: New-build yard soil check
text:
Why this matters
Topsoil is the layer where roots, water and soil life do most of their work. Subsoil compacted by trucks and graders can be as dense as a road base: roots can’t enter it and water can’t drain through it. Sod laid on a thin layer over it looks fine for a season, then thins out, browns in summer and floods after storms.
Fixing it costs far less before planting than after, so check before you invest in landscaping.

Example: making GIS depth-aware
GIS platforms treat soil as a stack of flat layers, so properties jump at every layer boundary and anything between the standard depths is lost. We built a physics-informed depth spline that runs inside Google Earth Engine, turning a spatially explicit platform into one that is also depth-aware. Each pixel carries a continuous, physically consistent profile, so properties can be read at any depth or integrated over the whole profile, and new layers such as moisture or temperature can be added to the same framework.

    Reading the results
    
      Nugget : sill is the share of variation you can't predict at your sampling scale: measurement error plus variation over distances shorter than your closest samples. Under 25% is strong spatial dependence, 25–75% moderate, over 75% weak.

      RMSE vs. the mean is the real test: it shows how much spatial prediction actually adds. A map made by kriging is only worth its colours if this is clearly above zero.
      MSDR and interval coverage show whether the uncertainty is honest. MSDR near 1 and coverage near 90% mean the kriging variance can be trusted; otherwise the uncertainty map is too optimistic or too cautious.
      Two limits that are rarely stated. Cross-validated RMSE can't fall much below the square root of the nugget, because that part of the variation isn't predictable from neighbours. And when samples are further apart than the range, RMSE approaches the standard deviation of the data. A published RMSE well below these limits usually means the validation points weren't independent of the calibration data, the variogram came from a different dataset, or the error was reported on a different scale.

      Reading the indices
      Richness counts classes. Shannon (H′) rises with both more classes and more even shares. Evenness (J′) is Shannon relative to its maximum for that many classes, from 0 (one class dominates) to 1 (all equal). Simpson is the chance that two random points fall in different classes.
      Hill numbers give the "effective number of classes": N1 weights classes by their share, N2 counts only the common ones. Dominance is the share of the most common class.
    
  
  
    Diversity is more than counting classes
    Taxonomic indices treat every class as equally different and ignore where soils sit and how they change with depth. Our approach measures pedodiversity from continuous soil properties in three dimensions, as the organisation of energy across the soil system.

title: Should I amend my soil?
text: Compost and topsoil are useful, but a lot of money goes on amendments that don’t help, or make things worse. Answer a few questions and this tells you what’s worth doing for what you’re planting.

title: Should I amend my soil?
text:
The short version

Trees: never amend the planting hole. Wide hole, native soil, mulch.
Native and low-water plants: usually nothing. Rich soil works against them.
Vegetables: yes, compost every year.
Lawns: improve the soil before seeding. On an existing lawn, aerate and top-dress lightly.
Clay: compost helps; a little sand makes it worse.
Standing water: a drainage problem, not a soil-quality one.

title: Raised bed and planter soil calculator
text: Filling raised beds and big planters takes more soil than most people expect, and bags add up fast. This works out the volume for beds, round pots and tree planters, and shows how to cut the cost of deep beds.

title: Raised bed and planter soil calculator
text:
Tips for filling beds

A raised bed 4 × 8 ft and 12 in deep holds about 1.2 cubic yards (32 ft³) once settled. That’s over 20 bags of 1.5 ft³.
Fill in layers and water each one so the soil settles before you plant.
Top up each spring. Beds sink as organic matter breaks down; an inch or two of compost each year keeps them full.
Avoid treated wood scraps as filler, and anything painted or glued.

title: Raised bed and planter soil calculator
text:
Pots and potting mix

Potting mix is sold in quarts or cubic feet in the US (8 qt, 16 qt, 1–2 cu ft) and in litres elsewhere. One cubic foot is about 26 quarts or 28 litres.
Nursery “gallon” sizes are trade sizes, not measurements. A #1 (“1-gallon”) pot holds about 3 quarts; a #5 holds about 4 gallons.
Use potting mix, not garden soil, in pots. Garden soil packs down in containers and stays waterlogged at the bottom.

title: Frost depth calculator
text:
In cold places the ground can freeze several feet down. Water lines, footings and fence posts set above that depth can burst, crack or get pushed up by frost heave. This estimates how deep frost goes in an average winter and a cold one, for your climate, surface and soil.
You need two numbers: the average temperature of your coldest month and of your warmest month. They are in the climate table for your town (on Wikipedia or your weather service). In the mountains, use a station at a similar elevation: temperatures drop about 3.5 °F per 1,000 ft (6.5 °C per 1,000 m) as you go up.

title: Frost depth calculator
section: Why frost depth varies so much
text:
Why frost depth varies so much

Cold, and how long it lasts. What matters is the freezing index: how far below freezing it is, added up over every day of winter. A long, steady cold freezes deeper than a short, sharp one.
Snow. A foot of fluffy snow insulates about as well as a couple of inches of foam board. Plowed driveways and shoveled paths lose that blanket and freeze deepest.
Soil and moisture. Water gives off a lot of heat as it freezes, which slows the frost. Dry gravel and rocky fill freeze much deeper than wet clay.
Warm ground below. Where summers are warm, the ground stores heat that pushes back against the frost from below.

title: Frost depth calculator
text:
About this estimate
This uses the same heat-flow physics as engineering frost-depth methods, with typical soil properties for each soil type. It is an estimate for an average and a colder-than-average winter, not a design value. Soil properties alone can shift the answer by about a quarter. Building codes set frost depths from the coldest winters in decades, so follow your local code for footings.
For more control (freezing index, density, water content and surface factors), use the frost depth tool for researchers.

title: Compost mix calculator (greens and browns)
text: A compost pile works fastest at a carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio of about 25–35 and moisture like a wrung-out sponge. Too much nitrogen (greens) and it smells; too much carbon (browns) and it barely heats up. Enter what you’re adding, by the bucket or any equal measure.

title: Compost mix calculator (greens and browns)
text:
Greens and browns

Greens (nitrogen-rich, usually wet): grass clippings, kitchen scraps, coffee grounds, fresh garden plants, manure.
Browns (carbon-rich, usually dry): dry leaves, straw, wood chips, sawdust, cardboard, newspaper.

Note that “parts” are by volume, and materials differ a lot in weight: a bucket of grass clippings weighs several times a bucket of dry leaves. That’s why roughly 2–3 buckets of browns to 1 of greens often balances.
Keep out: meat, dairy and oily food (attract pests), pet and human waste, diseased plants, weeds with seeds (unless your pile gets hot), and anything treated with herbicide. Some herbicides survive composting and damage vegetables.

text: RafikiArdhi is an independent environmental research company built on one idea: science should stay open. We publish what we produce, turn validated methods into free tools, and fund that work through the projects we take on.

title: About
text:
Open by design


We publish what we produce
Our methods go through peer review and into the scientific literature, with the details needed to reproduce them. Results that shape decisions should be open to scrutiny.


Free tools
Validated methods become free tools that anyone can use in a browser from the home gardener to the peer reviewer. They run on your own device, so your data never leaves it.


Paid work funds open work
Projects, advanced analyses and custom development pay for the research. As methods are proven, and agreements allow, they are released openly.


Credit where it is due
We build on other people’s work and cite it clearly: the methods, data and classification systems our tools rely on.

Solve. We take on environmental problems that existing methods handle poorly.
Validate. The method is tested against independent data and published.
Release. A simplified, well-documented version becomes a free tool.

Always free
Published methods and open-access papers, the online tools, their documentation and the references behind them.


Projects
Advanced and continuous versions of the tools, analysis of your data, custom development and training. Client data stays confidential, and client-funded results are never published without an agreement.

title: About
text:
Approach
We build on existing knowledge rather than replacing it. Every map and piece of information is updated, not reset; every estimate propagates its uncertainty; and every result is explained in terms the decision maker can use.
We do not use AI to replace human expertise. Where others reach for black-box AI, we use “glass box” functions: methods that are easy to interpret, scale to large problems, and are benchmarked against AI models.
